raw_response:
You can build a crawler in Java. The useful distinction is between the programming language and the mechanism used to obtain the data. Python is one language choice; Selenium is a browser-automation component, and its official examples support both Java and Python. Choosing Java therefore does not, by itself, remove Selenium's browser-control capabilities. [Selenium](https://www.selenium.dev/)

## Why Python is often recommended

Python can make a small extraction script convenient to write and revise. Its official tutorial describes interactive experimentation, high-level containers, and compact programs with fewer declarations. That supports a development-effort explanation, especially for small exploratory scripts. It does not establish that every programmer will work faster in Python, or that a Python crawler executes faster than a Java crawler. The opened tutorial is a current revision dated October 26, 2026, so it is contextual evidence rather than a verified snapshot of what the questioner could read on April 12, 2023. [Python tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3.11/tutorial/appetite.html)

Python also offers several distinct tools for the task. Requests handles HTTP and exposes response text or JSON; Beautiful Soup helps extract data from HTML or XML. Scrapy supplies a framework for crawling and structured extraction, with an example that follows pagination. These are concrete ecosystem options, not evidence that Java lacks equivalent basic capabilities or that Selenium is required. [Requests](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/stable/) · [Beautiful Soup](https://www.crummy.com/software/BeautifulSoup/bs4/doc/) · [Scrapy 2.8 overview](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.8/intro/overview.html)

## Why Selenium might be recommended

Selenium controls a browser: it can navigate, locate elements, enter text, click controls, and retrieve element text. Those operations are demonstrated in the project's public Java example. They are useful when obtaining the data involves browser interaction, rather than only fetching a response. They still need to be assembled into a crawler with the site's navigation and extraction rules. The source was inspected, not executed against a target site. [Official Java example](https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/getting_started/FirstScript.java)

A page using JavaScript does not automatically mean you must automate a browser. Scrapy's versioned documentation recommends first identifying where the data comes from and, when possible, reproducing the request that supplies it. Browser rendering or interaction is a conditional next option. That suggests a practical first step: inspect whether the desired records are in the returned HTML or a data response before choosing the collection mechanism. [Dynamic-content guidance](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.8/topics/dynamic-content.html)

## What disadvantages would Java introduce?

For a short one-off script, Java can involve more surrounding program structure. The official Selenium examples illustrate this: the Java example has imports, a class and a main method, while the Python example expresses the same basic navigation with fewer lines. This is an example of setup and editing overhead, not a measured universal disadvantage. Your existing fluency and project environment could outweigh it. [Selenium examples](https://www.selenium.dev/)

Java does not inherently require a complicated extraction program. The jsoup cookbook demonstrates fetching and parsing an HTML page and reading its title with a concise API. It also documents request settings such as cookies and timeouts. If the required data is already in the HTTP response, this is a relevant Java alternative to browser automation. [jsoup URL fetching](https://jsoup.org/cookbook/input/load-document-from-url)

The material inspected does not justify claims that Java is intrinsically worse at crawling, cannot handle dynamic pages, or is necessarily slower than Python. Conversely, it does not establish equal runtime performance. A performance choice would require the actual page workflow and workload; neither is supplied.

## How I would choose with the information given

1. If you already work comfortably in Java, start by checking jsoup for response-based HTML extraction, or the Java Selenium bindings for a browser workflow.
2. If you are equally comfortable in both languages and want to iterate on a small script, Python with Requests and Beautiful Soup is a reasonable starting point when the response contains the data.
3. If a browser is required, choose Java or Python Selenium according to the surrounding code and your fluency.
4. If you want a Python framework for following pages and producing structured records, evaluate Scrapy. Its 2.8 release predates this question. [Scrapy release notes](https://docs.scrapy.org/en/2.8/news.html)

These are conditional choices, because the question summary does not specify the site, scale, or existing skills. There is no stated mandatory language, prohibited library, platform requirement, or maintenance condition to use as an exclusion. The first unresolved fact is how the target delivers the data: an accessible response favors an HTTP-and-parser approach; a required browser workflow favors browser automation. A missing site description is not evidence that any of these documented tools violates the question's requirements.

Evidence limitations: jsoup's page carries a pre-question publication date, and Scrapy 2.8 is dated February 2, 2023. Other inspected pages are undated live material or explicitly later revisions, so exact historical feature/version availability has not been reconstructed. The unauthenticated GitHub code-search attempt failed; public code was subsequently located through web search and opened without authentication.
